sanskrit:
तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं भर्गो देवस्य धीमहि।
धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात्॥
transliteration:
tat savitur vareṇyaṁ bhargo devasya dhīmahi
dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt
translation: We meditate on the glorious radiance of the divine Savitr, the source of all light. May it inspire and awaken our minds.
meaning: This is a prayer not for wealth but for a clear, awakened mind. It asks the light that lights the sun to light our thinking too.

story.title: The seer Vishvamitra
story.text: This hymn is credited to the seer Vishvamitra, a king who gave up his throne to seek wisdom. Through long discipline he became a great rishi, and the Gayatri he received became one of the most chanted verses in India.

illustration.idea: A sage standing waist-deep in a river at sunrise, palms joined, facing a golden sun.

teaching.title: Ask for clarity
teaching.practice: At sunrise or when you start your day, take a moment to ask for a clear mind rather than a particular result.

test.question: What does the Gayatri Mantra ask for?
Which Veda contains this verse?

sanskrit:
इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुरथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान्।
एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः॥
transliteration:
indraṁ mitraṁ varuṇam agnim āhur atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān
ekaṁ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṁ yamaṁ mātariśvānam āhuḥ
translation: They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and the heavenly bird Garutman. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names: Agni, Yama, Matarishvan.
meaning: Different people use different names and paths for the same ultimate truth. This verse is a root of respect for many views.

story.title: The riddle hymn of Dirghatamas
story.text: This verse comes from a long hymn of riddles credited to the seer Dirghatamas, who tradition says was born blind. Though he could not see the world, he saw a deep truth: behind the many gods, there is one reality.

illustration.idea: An elderly seer with closed eyes, surrounded by faint symbols of fire, wind, sky and water merging into one light.

teaching.title: Listen for the one
teaching.practice: When you hear someone describe a belief different from yours today, look for the shared truth beneath the different words.

test.question: 'Ekam sat' means...
How do the wise speak of the one truth?

sanskrit:
नासदासीन्नो सदासीत्तदानीं नासीद्रजो नो व्योमा परो यत्।
किमावरीवः कुह कस्य शर्मन्नम्भः किमासीद्गहनं गभीरम्॥
transliteration:
nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt tadānīṁ nāsīd rajo no vyomā paro yat
kim āvarīvaḥ kuha kasya śarmann ambhaḥ kim āsīd gahanaṁ gabhīram
translation: Then there was neither non-existence nor existence. There was no air, nor sky beyond it. What covered it, and where? Who protected it? Was there water, deep and unfathomable?
meaning: One of the oldest scriptures in the world begins its story of creation with honest questions. Wonder, not certainty, is the starting point.

story.title: The hymn of creation
story.text: The Nasadiya Sukta asks how everything began. It ends by saying that perhaps even the one who watches over creation from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not know. It is an ancient invitation to keep asking.

illustration.idea: A vast dark cosmos with the first faint swirl of light, a tiny seated figure gazing up in wonder.

teaching.title: Stay curious
teaching.practice: Ask one big question today that you do not know the answer to, and enjoy not knowing for a while.

test.question: What is the Nasadiya Sukta about?
How does this hymn approach creation?

sanskrit:
सं गच्छध्वं सं वदध्वं सं वो मनांसि जानताम्।
देवा भागं यथा पूर्वे सञ्जानाना उपासते॥
transliteration:
saṁ gacchadhvaṁ saṁ vadadhvaṁ saṁ vo manāṁsi jānatām
devā bhāgaṁ yathā pūrve sañjānānā upāsate
translation: Walk together, speak together, let your minds be in harmony, just as the gods of old sat together in agreement to share their portion.
meaning: Communities thrive when people move, talk and think together. Harmony is something we practise, not just hope for.

story.title: The last hymn of the Rig Veda
story.text: This is part of the very last hymn of the Rig Veda. After more than a thousand hymns, the collection closes with a call for people to gather, speak and decide together in unity.

illustration.idea: A circle of villagers of all ages seated around a fire under the stars, talking and listening.

teaching.title: Listen to agree
teaching.practice: In one conversation today, listen fully before replying, and look for the point where you agree.

test.question: What does this verse ask people to do?
options: Walk and speak together in harmony

test.question: Where in the Rig Veda is this hymn found?
options: It is not in the Rig Veda

sanskrit:
आ नो भद्राः क्रतवो यन्तु विश्वतोऽदब्धासो अपरीतास उद्भिदः।
देवा नो यथा सदमिद्वृधे असन्नप्रायुवो रक्षितारो दिवेदिवे॥
transliteration:
ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvato 'dabdhāso aparītāsa udbhidaḥ
devā no yathā sadam id vṛdhe asann aprāyuvo rakṣitāro dive-dive
translation: Let noble thoughts come to us from every side, undeceived, unhindered and fresh. May the gods always be with us for our growth, ever watchful, protecting us day after day.
meaning: Keep your mind open. Good ideas can come from anywhere and anyone, and welcoming them is how we grow.

story.title: An open door for wisdom
story.text: This verse is credited to the seer Gotama Rahugana. Its opening line is often quoted as a motto for learning: let good thoughts come to us from all directions, not just from people we already agree with.

illustration.idea: A house with all its doors and windows open, beams of light entering from every direction.

teaching.title: Learn from someone unexpected
teaching.practice: Learn one good idea today from a person or place you would not usually turn to.

test.question: From where should noble thoughts come, according to this verse?
What is the main lesson of this verse?

sanskrit:
त्र्यम्बकं यजामहे सुगन्धिं पुष्टिवर्धनम्।
उर्वारुकमिव बन्धनान्मृत्योर्मुक्षीय मामृतात्॥
transliteration:
tryambakaṁ yajāmahe sugandhiṁ puṣṭi-vardhanam
urvārukam iva bandhanān mṛtyor mukṣīya māmṛtāt
translation: We worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, who nourishes all life. As a ripe cucumber is freed from its vine, may we be freed from death, and not from immortality.
meaning: When the time comes, may we let go as naturally as ripe fruit falls from the vine, free and complete, not torn away.

story.title: Markandeya and Yama
story.text: In the Puranas, the boy Markandeya was destined to die at sixteen. When Yama came for him, he clung to a Shiva linga and chanted this mantra. Shiva appeared, stopped Yama, and blessed the boy with endless life.

illustration.idea: A boy embracing a stone linga in a temple while a radiant figure of Shiva rises from it to face a startled Yama.

teaching.title: Ripen, then release
teaching.practice: Think of something you are ready to let go of. Instead of tearing it away, let it fall away gently today.

test.question: What image does this mantra use for liberation?
options: A ripe cucumber freed from its vine

test.question: In the story, who saved Markandeya?

translation: The Earth is my mother, and I am her child.
meaning: We belong to the Earth; it does not belong to us. Caring for nature is caring for family.

story.title: The hymn to Mother Earth
story.text: The Bhumi Sukta is a long hymn of over sixty verses praising the Earth for her mountains, rivers, forests and the many peoples who live on her. It asks her forgiveness for the harm we do when we dig into her.

illustration.idea: A child resting in the lap of a vast green landscape shaped like a mother, rivers flowing through her hair.

teaching.title: Care for your mother
teaching.practice: Do one thing for the Earth today: plant something, pick up litter, or use less plastic.

test.question: How does this verse describe the Earth?
Which Veda contains the Bhumi Sukta?

sanskrit:
ईशा वास्यमिदं सर्वं यत्किञ्च जगत्यां जगत्।
तेन त्यक्तेन भुञ्जीथा मा गृधः कस्यस्विद्धनम्॥
transliteration:
īśā vāsyam idaṁ sarvaṁ yat kiñca jagatyāṁ jagat
tena tyaktena bhuñjīthā mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam
translation: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord. Enjoy it through renunciation. Do not covet anyone's wealth.
meaning: Everything is sacred and nothing is truly ours. Enjoy life by holding it lightly, without greed.

story.title: The Upanishad inside a Veda
story.text: The Isha Upanishad is unusual: it is the final chapter of the Shukla Yajur Veda itself. In just eighteen verses, it brings the Vedic rituals to their inner meaning, beginning with this verse.

illustration.idea: A person holding a flower in an open palm, light passing through everything around them.

teaching.title: Hold it lightly
teaching.practice: Enjoy one thing you own today with gratitude, while remembering it is on loan to you.

test.question: According to this verse, the world is...
How should we enjoy the world?

sanskrit:
असतो मा सद्गमय।
तमसो मा ज्योतिर्गमय।
मृत्योर्मामृतं गमय॥
transliteration:
asato mā sad gamaya
tamaso mā jyotir gamaya
mṛtyor māmṛtaṁ gamaya
translation: Lead me from the unreal to the real. Lead me from darkness to light. Lead me from death to immortality.
meaning: Three short lines that sum up the whole spiritual journey: toward truth, toward understanding, toward what never dies.

story.title: A prayer for every journey
story.text: These lines come from one of the oldest Upanishads, where they are chanted as part of a Vedic ritual. Today they are sung in schools, homes and temples across India as a prayer for growth.

illustration.idea: A path leading from a dark forest toward a glowing dawn horizon, a single lamp-bearer walking along it.

teaching.title: One step toward light
teaching.practice: Replace one thing today that keeps you in 'darkness', a rumour, a doom-scroll, a grudge, with something that brings light.

test.question: 'Tamaso ma jyotir gamaya' means...
options: Lead me from darkness to light

test.question: How many requests are in this prayer?

sanskrit:
ॐ सह नाववतु। सह नौ भुनक्तु।
सह वीर्यं करवावहै।
तेजस्वि नावधीतमस्तु मा विद्विषावहै॥
transliteration:
oṁ saha nāv avatu, saha nau bhunaktu
saha vīryaṁ karavāvahai
tejasvi nāv adhītam astu mā vidviṣāvahai
translation: May we both be protected together. May we both be nourished together. May we work together with energy. May our study be full of light, and may we never resent each other.
meaning: Learning is a partnership. Teacher and student grow together when they share effort and respect.

story.title: The gurukul prayer
story.text: In the ancient gurukuls, forest schools, teacher and students chanted this prayer together before lessons. It asks for success not for the student alone but for both of them, and for harmony between them.

illustration.idea: A teacher and a few students seated under a tree in a forest school, hands joined, morning light filtering through leaves.

teaching.title: Learn together
teaching.practice: Teach someone one thing you know today, and ask them to teach you one thing back.

test.question: Who chants this prayer together?
What does the last line ask for?
options: That we never resent each other
